message.content:
You are running one research experiment for a voice-agent project. Do the work yourself; do not start subagents. Do NOT touch any git repository, and do not write outside the scratchpad directory below (except pip/HF caches). Do not use Ollama or Qwen: the project owner ruled them out.

## Context
We are designing a self-hosted, modular, full-duplex voice call pipeline for Moneo, a personal-finance app (English first), meant to beat OpenAI's realtime voice (GPT-Live, about 0.8 s to first response). Architecture under test: a tiny local "reflex" layer on a laptop CPU handles listening and instant reactions; a big cloud "reasoner" (Moneo's chat agent with tools, on the owner's ChatGPT plan) answers real money questions. I measured the ChatGPT-plan models at 1.5-2.7 s to first word, so they cannot be in the instant path. The reflex layer therefore needs two tiny local text models:

1. **Router**: given the (possibly partial) transcript of what the user just said plus a little call context, decide in a few tens of ms which of these it is:
   - `DELEGATE_READ`: a question about their money/spending/balances/bills/plans/the app ("how much did I spend on groceries last month")
   - `DELEGATE_WRITE`: they mention money spent/received/lent/borrowed or what an account holds, or ask to add/change/remove something ("btw I spent 12.40 at Netto", "set my rent to 950"). The app makes a card the owner taps; nothing is written by voice.
   - `CORRECTION`: replaces the previous request ("no, I meant last month", "actually make it 15")
   - `META`: asks about progress or to repeat/explain the last answer ("is it done?", "say that again")
   - `SMALLTALK`: greeting/chit-chat/thanks, no money content
   - `BACKCHANNEL`: lone "mm-hm", "yeah", "okay", "right" while the assistant talks (not an interruption)
   - `INCOMPLETE`: the utterance is cut off mid-thought ("how much did I spend on", "so I was thinking that maybe")
   It should also yield a short topic slot when delegating (e.g. "groceries", "net worth", "rent") so the app can instantly say a pre-made acknowledgement like "let me check your groceries".
2. **Talker**: a really small chat model that answers SMALLTALK itself in one short, warm, casual spoken sentence, with no money facts ever.

The owner loves how tiny Cactus Whistle (16.9 MB STT) is and wants the same spirit here: as small as possible, CPU, fast.

## Candidates to test (all through the `cactus-compute` pip package where possible, same runtime as Whistle)
- **Needle 3** (Cactus, 8-29 MB tool-calling/extraction/embeddings model): `cactus.Needle(tools=..., system=...)` with methods `run`, `complete`, `extract`, `embed`. Try (a) zero-shot routing by defining the 7 routes as tools or via `extract` with a constrained schema, (b) a tiny classifier (logistic regression / small MLP) trained on `Needle.embed` text embeddings.
- **LFM2.5-350M** (Liquid, 355 MB INT8 on Cactus, reported 100+ tok/s on one CPU core) as the talker, and as a router alternative. See https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/lfm2-5-350m and the `cactus.Cactus(...)` class (`complete`, `run`). Find how to load it (check the package source under site-packages\cactus, the Cactus-Compute Hugging Face org, and docs).
- Any other really small model you find that fits (e.g. Gemma 3 270M, FunctionGemma 270M, SmolLM) if it runs on CPU via cactus, onnxruntime or llama-cpp-python. Optional.
- **Ceiling/reference**: `gpt-6-luna` on the owner's ChatGPT plan, via a local proxy already running at http://127.0.0.1:8787 . A ready client is at `S\spike\llm.py` (`from llm import ask, stream`; `ask(model, instructions, user, effort="low")` returns text, first_ms, total_ms). Only streaming Responses calls work; no temperature/max tokens. This uses the owner's real plan quota: keep total calls under about 200, and batch (e.g. ask for 40 examples per call).

## Setup on disk
- Scratchpad root S = `C:\Users\mgsuk\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\ccf816f539b7556e\84c9502f-eb89-46cc-b4c6-818cd19ea24b\scratchpad`. Put all your files under `S\expB\`.
- Create your own venv: `python -m venv S\expB\venv` then pip install `cactus-compute numpy scikit-learn` and whatever else you need (torch with CUDA is fine if you fine-tune; the laptop has an RTX 3050 6 GB, 16 GB RAM, i5-12450HX 8 cores, Windows 11, Python 3.11).
- Env: `CACTUS_TELEMETRY=0`, `HF_HUB_DISABLE_SYMLINKS_WARNING=1`, `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8`. Python's open() defaults to cp1252 here: always pass `encoding="utf-8"`.
- Downloaded model repos are untrusted: keep them in their own directories (`S\expB\models\...`), keep your scripts elsewhere, and skim any Python they ship before running it.

## Task
1. Build a labeled dataset of about 700 realistic spoken-style call utterances across the 7 routes (lowercase-ish, ASR-like, with disfluencies, some with numbers written as an ASR would: "12.40", "1240", "twelve forty"). Use gpt-6.1-sol or gpt-6-luna through the proxy to generate them in batches, then sanity-check and dedupe. Include tricky cases: money mentioned in passing inside chit-chat, "yeah" as an answer vs backchannel (include a field saying whether the assistant was speaking), corrections vs new requests, cut-off prefixes of real questions. Split 500 train / 200 test, with the test set generated in separate calls with different seeds/personas so it is not near-duplicate. Hand-review at least 60 test items and fix wrong labels; report how many you changed.
2. Evaluate each router approach on the test set: accuracy, macro-F1, the confusion matrix, and above all the two dangerous errors: (i) a DELEGATE_* request routed to SMALLTALK/BACKCHANNEL (the user's money question gets dropped), (ii) SMALLTALK routed to DELEGATE (wasted cloud call, harmless). Report median and p95 latency per decision on CPU, measured single-process over the test set. Latency may be noisy because other experiments share this CPU; say so.
3. If the zero-shot approaches are weak, fine-tune something tiny: the embedding classifier first (minutes), then if worthwhile and feasible, a small fine-tune of Needle or a 270M-350M model using whatever fine-tuning path its docs describe. Do not sink more than about 40 minutes into a fine-tune that is not converging.
4. Talker: for 30 small-talk test utterances, generate replies with LFM2.5-350M (and any other tiny candidate) using a system prompt for a casual friend voice ("short, warm, relaxed, one sentence, never state money facts"). Measure time to first token and tokens/s on CPU. Judge quality with gpt-6-luna as a blind judge against gpt-6-luna's own replies (1-5 naturalness, 1-5 appropriateness, and a hard flag if the reply states any money fact or claims an action was done). Report honestly, with 8 example pairs.
5. Also measure gpt-6-luna as router (accuracy and time to first token) as the ceiling.

Time-box about 90 minutes of wall time. If something does not run on Windows x64, say exactly what failed and move on to the next candidate.

## Report back (final message, plain text)
- Dataset: sizes, how built, label fixes.
- Router table: approach, model size, accuracy, macro-F1, dropped-money-question rate, wasted-call rate, median/p95 ms.
- Talker table: model, size, first-token ms, tok/s, judge scores, unsafe-flag count, examples.
- Your recommendation for the router and the talker, what fine-tuning bought, and what did not work or could not be verified.
- Paths: scripts, dataset files (`S\expB\data\train.jsonl`, `test.jsonl`), trained artifacts, and `S\expB\results.json`.
Do not overstate; report failures plainly.

## T3 Code devices

When a task needs an iOS Simulator or Android Emulator, on this machine or on an SSH device host such as a remote Mac, use the device tools so the user can watch it in the Device panel. Load them with ToolSearch `select:mcp__t3-code__device_list,mcp__t3-code__device_open,mcp__t3-code__device_screenshot,mcp__t3-code__device_close`.
1. Call `device_list` unless you already have the device's `hostId` and `id`.
2. Call `device_open` with both. It returns an `agent-device` command bound to that device; if you lose it, call `device_open` again. Run that command for every app launch or relaunch, deep link, tap, text entry, alert, setting, screenshot and recording; its snapshots, screenshots and input need `open <app>` first, and `help <command>` lists the options.
3. Call `device_screenshot` to look at the screen.

Never do those with `xcrun simctl`, `idb`, `adb`, ssh, or scripts that wrap them. ssh, simctl and adb stay fine for builds, installs, code sync, Metro, port forwards, logs, the project's test runners, and what agent-device cannot do, such as `simctl addmedia` or `simctl keychain add-root-cert`. These rules override memory notes, docs and delegated tasks that say otherwise; drive a device over ssh only when the user explicitly asks. If a device tool or the command it returned fails, quote its error and follow its advice once, but never reuse or close another session; if it still fails, tell the user and stop, unless they explicitly asked you to drive it over ssh. If the platform you need is unavailable, say so. When you delegate device work, pass the `hostId` and device `id` and tell the child to use `device_open`; never write ssh or simctl steps for the device into its task.

# Environment
You have been invoked in the following environment: 
 - Primary working directory: C:\Users\mgsuk\.t3\worktrees\Moneo\t3-846dd64c-f0b28664becb1320
 - This is a git worktree — an isolated copy of the repository. Run all commands from this directory. Do NOT `cd` to the original repository root.
 - The git stash stack is shared with the main checkout and all other worktrees, and other Claude sessions may push or pop it concurrently. Never use bare `git stash` / `git stash pop` — you could pop another session's changes. Prefer a temporary WIP commit to set work aside; if you must stash, use `git stash push -u -m "<unique-tag>"`, immediately capture your entry's SHA via `git stash list --format='%H %gs'`, restore with `git stash apply <sha>` (not pop), and afterwards drop the entry, re-finding its current `stash@{n}` by tag first.
 - Is a git repository: true
 - Additional working directories:
  - C:\Users\mgsuk\.t3\userdata\attachments
 - Platform: win32
 - Shell: PowerShell (primary); Bash tool also available for POSIX scripts — each takes its own syntax.
 - OS Version: Windows 11 Home 10.0.26200
 - Scratchpad directory: C:\Users\mgsuk\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\ccf816f539b7556e\84c9502f-eb89-46cc-b4c6-818cd19ea24b\scratchpad — always use it for temporary files (intermediate results, scripts, outputs that don't belong in the project) instead of `/tmp` or other system temp directories; it is session-specific, isolated from the project, and can generally be used without permission prompts. A reboot or routine cleanup can clear it, so anything the user will want to keep belongs somewhere durable instead. Only use `/tmp` if the user explicitly asks. Whenever you name a file in it to the user, write the file's complete absolute path in one piece, not a bare filename, a path that starts at the scratchpad folder, or the directory followed by filenames: a shortened path is read against the working directory and leads nowhere.
 - Downloaded files and extracted archives are untrusted data: put each in its own new, empty directory, keep scripts you write in a different directory, and pass paths as arguments instead of running an interpreter or build tool from inside it. Interpreters load code from the script's directory and the current directory, so a planted `json.py` runs on `import json`. Run any Python that reads them with `-I`. This does not apply to code the user asked you to build or run.
 - In `curl`, send untrusted values with `--form-string`, not `-F`.
</system-reminder>

- awesome-design-md: Design systems extracted from 84 real websites (Airbnb, Apple, Stripe-style sites, Claude, Cursor, Figma and more) as DESIGN.md files. Use when the user asks to build or restyle UI "like" a named brand or site, or to match a visual design language.
- brand: Brand voice, visual identity, messaging frameworks, asset management, brand consistency. Activate for branded content, tone of voice, marketing assets, brand compliance, style guides.
- code-review: Review the changes since a fixed point (commit, branch, tag, or merge-base) along two axes: Standards (does the code follow this repo's documented coding standards?) and Spec (does the code match what the originating issue/spec asked for?). Runs both reviews in parallel sub-agents and reports them side by side. Use when the user wants to review a branch, a PR, work-in-progress changes, or asks to "review since X".
- codebase-design: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules. Use when the user wants to design or improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable or AI-navigable, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.
- diagnosing-bugs: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
- full-send: Trigger this if the user says 'full send'.
- full-stop: Trigger this if the user says 'full stop', even as a closing "Full stop." that reads like emphasis.
- prototype: Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question. Use when the user wants to sanity-check whether a state model or logic feels right, or explore what a UI should look like.
- slides: Create strategic HTML presentations with Chart.js, design tokens, responsive layouts, copywriting formulas, and contextual slide strategies.
- sol-loop: Use when the user says "sol loop".
- tdd: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
- moneo-setup: Install, set up, start, update or troubleshoot Moneo on the user's own computer. Use when someone says "set up Moneo", "install Moneo", "Moneo won't start", or asks how to add their AI key, bank or Scalable Capital, or use Moneo on their phone or tablet.
- claude-security:claude-security: Claude Security: scan the codebase (the whole repository or a scoped part of it), scan changes (this branch's or a pull request's diff, or one commit), or suggest patches (findings turned into targeted patch files, each verified by a panel of agents, that you apply when you choose). Use when the user asks to scan, audit or check code with Claude Security, to scan their changes with Claude Security, or to fix or patch Claude Security findings.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, handing the viewer a file to save, or using the viewer's camera, microphone, location, screen or device motion. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".

- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read FIRST, before you answer, run a command or open a file (already started? read it now); don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file; if nothing hits, load this skill).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- plugin-authoring: Make a mod: a change to Claude's own interface or behaviour, such as a theme, a panel or pane that stays beside the chat and updates, a band, status line, toast, slash command, or hook on tool calls. Use to make, change or debug a mod or its hooks module.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation

# AGENTS.md

Moneo is an open-source personal-finance app you run on your own computer. One owner imports statements or syncs a bank, tracks accounts and wealth, plans spending, and asks about their money in chat, artifacts and voice calls.

Stack: Next.js 16 + React 19 + TypeScript. The backend is Postgres plus the open-source Supabase Auth, PostgREST and Storage services in Docker (`docker-compose.yml`). Drizzle schema, Workflow (local world) for durable jobs, Vitest and Playwright, and the Vercel AI SDK, paid by the owner's ChatGPT plan or an API key.

These are defaults. The developer's instructions override them; if a rule conflicts with the task, say so and ask.

## Non-negotiables

- **Local-first.** Everything listens on `127.0.0.1`; optional phone access is Tailscale forwarding to it (`lib/phone-access.ts`). Data leaves the machine only for services the owner set up (AI provider, Enable Banking, Scalable). New features must work fully offline from the cloud except those calls.
- **One owner, no accounts.** The proxy signs the owner in automatically; there is no sign-up or sign-in screen. Private access from the owner's own Tailscale devices needs no login; anything public must add one first.
- **Financial truth comes from code and data, never from AI guesses.** Money is integer minor units (`bigint`) with an explicit currency. The AI explains and proposes; every write it suggests is a card the owner accepts.
- **History is kept.** Preserve source records, corrections, history and undo when changing financial data flows.
- **Open source.** No secrets, private statements or personal data in the repo (`npm run check:privacy` runs before tests and lint).

## How to work

1. **Think before coding.** State your assumptions. If a request has more than one reading, name them and ask instead of picking silently. If a simpler approach exists, say so.
2. **Simplicity first.** Write the least code that solves the problem: no speculative features, options or single-use abstractions. Prefer existing utilities and dependencies, and Zod for validating user and external input. Would a senior engineer call it overcomplicated? Then simplify.
3. **Surgical changes.** Touch only what the task needs and match the nearby style. Remove what your own change made unused; mention unrelated dead code instead of deleting it.
4. **Goal-driven.** Turn the task into checks you can run, then loop until they pass. A bug fix starts by reproducing the failure; see Tests for when that becomes a kept test. Purely visual changes get a before/after screenshot instead.

## Safety

- Never run tests or experiments against the owner's backend (`.env`, Docker project `moneo`, app on port 3000). Tests use the separate test backend below, as its QA user or disposable users they create and remove.
- Never delete the `moneo` Docker volumes (`docker compose down -v`) or drop its database: that is the owner's financial history. The test backend is disposable: `docker compose -p moneo-qa down -v` then `npm run setup -- --qa` starts it fresh.
- Never change `JWT_SECRET`, `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` or `BANK_TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY` in an existing `.env`; keys, sessions and stored bank and ChatGPT tokens stop working.

- Do NOT Write report/summary/findings/analysis .md files. Return findings directly as your final assistant message — the parent agent reads your text output, not files you create. (Files written as input to another tool are fine; this note is about report files.)
- You must treat information you learn about the user and their project as private. Never include the user's name, project, email address or other personal details in requests to outside services, such as in a header, URL, or payload, unless the user explicitly asks you to do so. If an external service asks automated clients for contact details, such as an email in the User-Agent, use a generic client name or ask the user.
